newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Wall St fears escalation in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Wall St fears escalation in Gulf.

text.p: If the latest conflict between the United States and Iraq escalates, Wall Street pros will find themselves scampering away from stocks that could take a beating.

Analysts said the effect on the stock market from Thursday's renewed tensions in the Persian Gulf has been minimal so far, but market players were keeping a nervous eye on Iraq for any warning that oil prices could shoot up, which would send equities and bonds lower.

These latest worries come at a delicate time for the stock market, which on Thursday saw the Dow Industrials in record territory. Inflation worries have arisen from strong economic data and upward pressure on wages.
The Dow Industrials closed up 17.02 points, or 0.30 percent, at 5771.94 on Thursday.

"The price of oil will tell you what the stock market will do," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "If the price of oil does go up it will be like a tax on the U.S. economy and strategists will have to evaluate what the effect of that tax on corporate earnings will be."
Oil drives many stocks and sectors, affecting people at the gas pump and in the kitchen and is the lifeblood of airlines and major industrial companies.
"It's a long, long list," Johnson said, referring to stocks which could take a drubbing if oil prices were to soar.

Analysts see the current situation as a double-edged sword. They say that, if the conflict reached a stage at which it would interupt the flow of oil from countries other than Iraq, it could cause a slowdown in economic activity and the reactivation of inflation psychology.

"The biggest possible problem is the interuption of oil supplies. That would be a profound negative and lead to a furious slowdown in economic activity throughout the industrialized world combined with an exacerbation of inflation psychology from higher oil prices," Metz said.
Metz further said that, as long the conflict was confined to Iraq, it was not a major economic problem.
"But we are seeing resistance by Saudi Arabia and Turkey to our actions, so we are in a no-win situation. The alliance has disintegrated and that creates a major problem."
On the other hand, a rise in oil prices could also, to some extent, benefit U.S. market players for whom it would represent a welcome slowdown in the economy.
"I think Wall Street is keeping one eye at most on what is going on in the Gulf. But, obviously, people are watching and worrying," Johnson said.
"If the conflict intensifies, the odds are that it will be much longer before we see the 600,000 to 800,000 barrels of per day from Iraq."

He said the situation was either not being treated seriously on Wall Street, or is "seen as a factor that could help slow the U.S. economy. In other words, a rise in oil prices is not yet considered a threat to the economy."
Iraq said on Thursday that its air defense units fired three missiles at U.S. and Allied warplanes patrolling the no-fly zone in southern Iraq.
But the Pentagon has said it had no reports from its units in the field that Iraq had fired the missiles.
Oil stocks failed to respond to Thursday's events with Texaco Inc down 7/8 at 93-3/4, Mobil Corp down two at 116-3/8, Chevron Corp unchanged at 61-1/2. Exxon Corp was up 1/4 at 85.
